description.narrative:
According to INAM, from November 2023 to February 2024, the southern and central regions of the country registered a deficit in precipitation. In January 2024, there were more than 23 consecutive days without significant precipitation in the southern andcentral parts of the country. Severe seasonal deficits were recorded in Manica, Nampula, Sofala, Tete and Zambezia. Some 1.25 million people were already food insecure (IPC3+) in areas that have been impacted by severe drought conditions during the 2023/24 rainy and agricultural season. These people will likely see their food insecurity situation deteriorate and fall into severe and emergency food insecurity (IPC4+). FEWSNET warns that Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected to emerge in semi-arid districts of Gaza, Inhambane, Manica, Sofala, and Tete. The Government of Mozambique is working with different partners, including some from the UN, in implementing Anticipatory Actions; for the first time the Government approved the activation of Anticipatory Action Plans for nine districts (five in Gaza, two in Tete and two in Sofala) to mitigate the effects of the drought. The coverage of this effort is insufficient as compared to the needs; more resources are needed to scale-up interventions. The foodsecurity situation in Mozambique is likely to deteriorate due the compounded effects of El Niño which brought above-average temperatures, persistent dryness with many areas receiving less than half of their typical rainfall. These events in turn led to deteriorating vegetation conditions and crop wilting in parts of the south and central provinces. Food prices are likely to remain high due to the prospect of yet another below-average harvest in 2024-2025. FEWSNET estimates that some 690,000 hectares ofcrops (15 per cent of total planted area) mainly in southern and central parts of the country have been damaged by extreme weather events, leading to below-average harvests. Also, according to FEWSNET,supplies from the 2024 cereal harvest are expected to be insufficient to cover regional requirements for Marketing Year (MY) 2024/25 due to extended dry periods, high temperatures, and early end of the rainy season driven by El Niño conditions. Mozambique is expected to be 41 per cent below the five-year average. It is to be noted that some areas in the south are still struggling to recover from the floods while in the centre extensive dry spells followed by the cyclone Feddy. Faced with this situation, Oxfam and its partner (AJOAGO) propose to support the response to food insecurity induced by the El Ninõ Phenomenon, through Food Assistance, WASH andawareness sessions on safe programming and protection risks in 3 three districts in the north of Gaza Province, namely: Massangena,Chigubo and Chicualacuala,Southern Mozambique. Since 2001, AJOAGO has been involved in successful DRR, preparedness and emergency responses, improving water, sanitation and hygiene services, food security and other programs in rural communities in Mozambique. Outputs and activities proposed: Output 1: Food Security and Vulnerable Livelihoods response activities by Oxfam and its partners ensure adequate food access for affected families and improve the functioning of local markets. Activity 1. Community mobilization for fooddistribution (dissemination of selection criteria, etc.): Activity 2. Food distribution to the families in the resettlement centers and or/host communities. Activity 3. Nutrition education promotion messages at distributions points. Activity 4. Restore the productive capacity of families (distribution of seeds of drought-tolerant crops) Activity 5. Post food distribution monitoring (PDM). Output 2: Ensure that Oxfam and its partners' WaSH initiatives result in access to safe water and sanitation andcontribute to improving hygiene conditions for drought-affected households in target districts. WASH interventions will prioritize and target: 1. WASH services in healthcare facilities and/or in their communities in severely affected districts (including cholera treatment centres). 2. People living in areas with reduced access to water (related to the drought) for domestic and livelihoods. 3. WASH provisions in vulnerable schools. Emergency Measures: 1. Provision of emergency water services to communities, schools, health facilities. • Rehabilitation of existing water systems • Limited water trucking in the most urgent scenarios (in healthcare facilities, CTCs.) 2. Provision emergency sanitation services health facilities (especially cholera treatment centers. • Rehabilitation of existing institutional sanitation facilities. • Limited emergency latrines in highly impacted health centers/ cholera treatment centers. 3. Distribution ofcritical hygiene supplies (water treatment chemicals, safe waterstorage containers, soap, etc.). Building resilient WASH services: 1. Provision of resilient safe water services to communities, health facilities and schools facing water insecurity by:. • rehabilitation of existing water systems, including solar-powered multi-use water systems that apply an integrated livelihood and domestic water use approach. • increasing water storage capacity (cisterns rehabilitation, poly tanks, etc) at community and institution levels(health facilities and schools). • promoting the productive use of surface water and groundwater. 2. Improve the use of basic sanitation services for communities, health facilities and schools facing water insecurity by: • Rehabilitation of existing institutionalsanitation facilities. •Increasing sanitation coverage at the household level through PEC (Participação e Educação Comunitário). 3.Ensuring the provision critical hygiene supplies (water treatment chemicals, safe water storage containers, soap, etc.) to health facilities and schools as well as vulnerable families in drought-affected districts. 4. Hygiene promotion and encourage safe sanitation practices including water conservation actions through established community health and hygiene mechanisms as well as mass media. 5.Strengthen technical capacity of decentralized authorities for oversight and adherence to technical construction and management standards to enable resilient water supply systems (ie pump testing, minimum water yields for development, ‘secure’ casing, sanitaryseals, informed depths, etc.). 6. Strengthen effective engagement in coordination mechanisms at the national and sub-national levels,with strong links in particular to Food Security, Health <(>&<)> Nutrition, and Education coordination arrangements.
Output 3: Ensure safe programming and mitigate gender and protection risks in reducing the risk and vulnerabilities of the most vulnerable population groups in the community. Activities: - Community awareness on protection against sexual abuse and exploitation. - Participate in Protection Cluster meetings. - Train community members on community-based reporting and feedback mechanisms. - Train community leaders and activists on protection against sexual abuse and exploitation. - Establish protectionfocal points at community level to follow up on cases. - Promotion of hygiene messages during the distribution of hygiene kits. - Link VBG or VCMR to district referral paths. - Awareness raising and regular monitoring of protection and risks of sexualexploitation and abuse in resettlement centers and/or host communities. - Establishment of community-based reporting/complaints and feedback mechanisms.
